extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI) and third-party assessment by a notified body based on quality management system and technical documentation assessment (Annex VII).

In the 2021 and November 2022 proposal texts of Article 43(1), for high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider's choice of procedure depended on whether harmonised standards or common specifications had been applied.
Under the current (service desk) text of Article 43, for high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, a distinct procedure applies (text available is truncated in sources).

A provider may choose any notified body for conformity assessment, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority under Article 74(8) or (9) must act as the notified body.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU product safety legislation listed in Annex I Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures under that existing legislation, with notified bodies also verifying the AI-specific requirements of the AI Act.

A substantial modification to a high-risk AI system requires a new conformity assessment, unless the modification was predetermined by the provider at the time of the initial assessment (relevant to systems that continue to learn after deployment).

Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority to derogate from the Article 43 conformity assessment procedure and authorise placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system for a limited period, for exceptional reasons of public security, life/health protection, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Annex VII, point 4.5, provides that a notified body may be granted access to the training and trained models of an AI system, including relevant parameters, when necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 requirements and after other reasonable means have proven insufficient, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

Annex VI is described by industry commentary as a self-assessment (internal control) procedure not requiring a notified body, and is said to be usable by most high-risk AI systems not embedded in Annex I regulated products.
Industry commentary states that Annex VII (notified body involvement) is mandatory specifically for biometric identification systems and certain critical infrastructure AI systems.

As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for AI Act conformity assessments was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity, ahead of an August 2026 deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated in connection with the AI Act/MDR-IVDR interplay for medical device AI systems.

Commentary indicates that notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments only after 2026, intersecting with existing MDR/IVDR notified body assessments.

As of October 2025, the Commission's NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR); these designations are under MDR/IVDR, not the AI Act itself.

A Council document (ST-7322-2026-INIT) and a Commission document (COM(2025) 836, ST-15708-2025-INIT) describe draft codes/categories and a proposed new Annex XIV intended to integrate AI Act high-risk conformity assessment body designation into the Commission's NANDO information system, indicating this specific integration framework was still at the proposal stage as of those documents.

Under the separate Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), which began applying in part on 11 June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated in the NANDO database as of late June 2026, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by 11 December 2026 and full application from 11 December 2027; this is a distinct regulation from the AI Act.
A blog-style checklist asserts that every high-risk AI system needs an 'algorithm passport' registered with the AI Office before first use, presented as a legal requirement.

contradictions.claim_a: For Annex III point 1 (biometric) systems, the provider's choice of conformity assessment procedure depends on whether harmonised standards/common specifications were applied (per 2021/2022 proposal texts of Article 43).
contradictions.claim_b: The current service-desk text of Article 43 frames notified body choice primarily around exceptions for law enforcement/immigration/asylum/EU institution use cases, without reiterating the harmonised-standards-dependent choice language from the earlier proposals.
contradictions.description: Sources 14 and 19 reflect the 2021 and November 2022 proposal versions of Article 43, while sources 11, 12, and 13 reflect the AI Act Service Desk's presentation of the (later, adopted) Article 43 text; the proposal and current-text framings differ in how the Annex III point 1 procedural choice is described, and it is unclear from the excerpts provided whether this reflects a substantive change in the final Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 or simply a difference in how each source excerpts the article.

contradictions.claim_a: Every high-risk AI system needs an 'algorithm passport' registered with the AI Office before first use, stated as a legal requirement.
contradictions.claim_b: The AI Act's documented conformity assessment and market-entry requirements (Article 43 internal control/notified body assessment, Article 47 EU declaration of conformity, Article 48 CE marking, Article 49 registration) make no mention of any 'algorithm passport' requirement.
contradictions.description: Source 15 asserts a specific named legal requirement ('algorithm passport') that is not corroborated by any official EU guidance, legal text, or other independent source describing Article 43-49 obligations; this appears to be an unsupported or fabricated claim inserted into an otherwise generic compliance checklist, and should not be treated as an actual legal requirement under the AI Act.

open_issues: No source provides a definitive, dated count of notified bodies formally designated specifically under the EU AI Act (as opposed to under MDR/IVDR or the unrelated Cyber Resilience Act) as of the current date (October 2026).

It is unclear whether the proposed new Annex XIV / NANDO integration described in the Council and Commission documents (sources 8 and 9) has been formally adopted, and if so, on what date, and how it affects the designation of AI Act-specific conformity assessment bodies.

The exact current status and finalized text of Article 43's procedural distinctions (e.g., for Annex III point 1 versus points 2-8) is not fully available in the sources, which are truncated, making it hard to confirm whether the proposal-stage conditional logic (tied to harmonised standards) survived into the final adopted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

Sources do not clarify the practical timeline or process by which Member States are expected to complete AI Act notified body designations relative to the August 2026 high-risk AI obligations deadline.

The claim in source 15 regarding an 'algorithm passport' requirement is not verified by any other source and its origin/legal basis is unclear; it may be inaccurate or fabricated and should be independently verified against the official Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 text.

Sources do not clarify how conformity assessments already completed for medical devices or other Annex I products under existing legislation (MDR/IVDR) will be practically reconciled with the still-developing AI Act-specific notified body designations.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two distinct routes to demonstrate conformity for high-risk AI systems: internal control and third-party assessment by a notified body, with the applicable route depending on the system's Annex III category or its overlap with existing product-safety legislation (high confidence). However, the notified body ecosystem specifically designated for AI Act assessments remains underdeveloped and poorly documented, with sources unable to confirm any formally designated AI Act notified bodies as of the research date, despite an approaching August 2026 compliance deadline (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, and third-party assessment by a notified body based on quality management system and technical documentation review under Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43), [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product safety legislation listed in Annex I Section A—such as medical devices and machinery—providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures under that existing legislation, with notified bodies also verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

Under the current service-desk text, a distinct procedure applies to high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, though the available excerpts are truncated and the precise mechanics are unclear (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Earlier 2021 and November 2022 proposal texts indicated that for Annex III point 1 systems (biometric identification), the provider's choice of procedure depended on whether harmonised standards or common specifications had been applied—but it is uncertain whether this logic survived into the final adopted Regulation (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [Artificial-Intelligence-Act.com](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)).

Providers may generally choose any notified body, except that systems intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions must use the relevant market surveillance authority as the notified body under Article 74(8)/(9) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). A substantial modification to a high-risk AI system requires a new conformity assessment unless predetermined by the provider at initial assessment—relevant to continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from Article 43 procedures and authorise temporary market placement for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructural reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Annex VII, point 4.5, allows notified bodies access to training and trained models, including parameters, when necessary and after other means prove insufficient, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

Industry commentary (lower reliability) describes Annex VI as a self-assessment route usable by most high-risk systems not embedded in Annex I regulated products, and asserts Annex VII notified-body involvement is mandatory specifically for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems (low confidence) ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

### Notified Body Designations
No source confirms a definitive count of notified bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself. As of October 2025, the Commission's NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies under the Medical Devices Regulation and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation—but these are MDR/IVDR designations, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). Council and Commission documents describe a proposed new Annex XIV intended to integrate AI Act notified-body designation into NANDO, indicating this framework remained at proposal stage (medium confidence) ([Council ST-7322-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf), [COM(2025) 836](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). Lower-reliability blog sources suggest that, as of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem was still being built with limited capacity ahead of an August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and that as of April 2026 no notified bodies had been designated for the AI Act/MDR-IVDR interplay for medical AI (low confidence) ([AI Act Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Proposal-era texts (2021/2022) and the current service-desk text describe Annex III point 1 procedural choices differently; it is unclear whether this reflects a genuine legislative change or inconsistent excerpting (low confidence claims involved). One source asserts a legal requirement for an "algorithm passport" registered with the AI Office before first use; this is uncorroborated by any official source and should be treated as unverified or potentially fabricated (low confidence, 0.12) ([unverified checklist](https://ai-compliance-hub.example/high-risk-ai-checklist)). Multiple low-confidence claims (0.12–0.14) regarding notified body timelines rely solely on single blog sources and lack official corroboration.

## Knowledge Gaps
No dated, authoritative count of AI Act-specific notified bodies exists. The adoption status of the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration is unclear. The final text of Article 43's Annex III point 1 vs. points 2–8 distinction needs verification against Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The practical reconciliation between existing MDR/IVDR assessments and AI Act-specific requirements remains undocumented.

2. [Article 46 | AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two distinct routes to demonstrate conformity for high-risk AI systems: internal control and third-party assessment by a notified body, with the applicable route depending on the system's Annex III category or its overlap with existing product-safety legislation (high confidence). However, the notified body ecosystem specifically designated for AI Act assessments remains underdeveloped and poorly documented, with sources unable to confirm any formally designated AI Act notified bodies as of the research date, despite an approaching August 2026 compliance deadline (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, and third-party assessment by a notified body based on quality management system and technical documentation review under Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43), [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product safety legislation listed in Annex I Section A—such as medical devices and machinery—providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures under that existing legislation, with notified bodies also verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

Under the current service-desk text, a distinct procedure applies to high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, though the available excerpts are truncated and the precise mechanics are unclear (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Earlier 2021 and November 2022 proposal texts indicated that for Annex III point 1 systems (biometric identification), the provider's choice of procedure depended on whether harmonised standards or common specifications had been applied—but it is uncertain whether this logic survived into the final adopted Regulation (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [Artificial-Intelligence-Act.com](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)).

Providers may generally choose any notified body, except that systems intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions must use the relevant market surveillance authority as the notified body under Article 74(8)/(9) (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). A substantial modification to a high-risk AI system requires a new conformity assessment unless predetermined by the provider at initial assessment—relevant to continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from Article 43 procedures and authorise temporary market placement for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructural reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Annex VII, point 4.5, allows notified bodies access to training and trained models, including parameters, when necessary and after other means prove insufficient, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

Industry commentary (lower reliability) describes Annex VI as a self-assessment route usable by most high-risk systems not embedded in Annex I regulated products, and asserts Annex VII notified-body involvement is mandatory specifically for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems (low confidence) ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

### Notified Body Designations
No source confirms a definitive count of notified bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself. As of October 2025, the Commission's NANDO database listed 51 notified bodies under the Medical Devices Regulation and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation—but these are MDR/IVDR designations, not AI Act designations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). Council and Commission documents describe a proposed new Annex XIV intended to integrate AI Act notified-body designation into NANDO, indicating this framework remained at proposal stage (medium confidence) ([Council ST-7322-2026-INIT](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf), [COM(2025) 836](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)). Lower-reliability blog sources suggest that, as of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem was still being built with limited capacity ahead of an August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)), and that as of April 2026 no notified bodies had been designated for the AI Act/MDR-IVDR interplay for medical AI (low confidence) ([AI Act Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Proposal-era texts (2021/2022) and the current service-desk text describe Annex III point 1 procedural choices differently; it is unclear whether this reflects a genuine legislative change or inconsistent excerpting (low confidence claims involved). One source asserts a legal requirement for an "algorithm passport" registered with the AI Office before first use; this is uncorroborated by any official source and should be treated as unverified or potentially fabricated (low confidence, 0.12) ([unverified checklist](https://ai-compliance-hub.example/high-risk-ai-checklist)). Multiple low-confidence claims (0.12–0.14) regarding notified body timelines rely solely on single blog sources and lack official corroboration.

## Knowledge Gaps
No dated, authoritative count of AI Act-specific notified bodies exists. The adoption status of the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration is unclear. The final text of Article 43's Annex III point 1 vs. points 2–8 distinction needs verification against Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The practical reconciliation between existing MDR/IVDR assessments and AI Act-specific requirements remains undocumented.
